title: Block: A 1-D DP Table (Bottom-Up)
oneLiner: Find the cheapest way to climb a staircase taking one or two steps at a time, filling a table from the bottom.
keyTakeaway: Bottom-up DP: say what dp[i] means in one sentence, fill the base cases, then fill each entry from the ones before it. Most 1-D DP bugs are an unclear meaning for dp[i].
explanation:
cost[i] is what it costs to stand on step i (there are at least two steps). You can start on step 0 or step 1, and from any step climb one or two. Return the cheapest total to get past the last step. [10, 15, 20] costs 15: start on step 1 and climb two.

Let dp[i] be the cheapest total to stand on step i. dp[0] = cost[0] and dp[1] = cost[1]; after that dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2]). The top is reached from either of the last two steps, so the answer is the smaller of those two. House Robber, Fibonacci and Decode Ways are this block with a different recurrence, and two variables can replace the array once it works.

starterCode.python:
def min_cost_climb(cost):
    # 1. Make dp the same length as cost: dp[i] is the cheapest total to stand on step i.
    # 2. Fill the base cases: dp[0] = cost[0], dp[1] = cost[1].
    # 3. For each later step, dp[i] = cost[i] + the smaller of dp[i - 1] and dp[i - 2].
    # 4. The top is reached from either of the last two steps: return the smaller of those.
    return 0

gotchas: Returning dp[n - 1] instead of the smaller of the last two entries.
Starting the loop at 1 and reading dp[-1].

complexity.note: One pass with O(1) work per step; the table is n long, or two variables if you keep only the last two entries.
